Trap
trap
n. (a snare; a device hidden to catch a living thing)
Saxon treppe. A trap differs from a net in being hidden and in being sprung by the victim's own movement — which is exactly how Scripture uses it, of tables, of ways, and of men who set them for other men.

Biblical Definition

“Let their table become a snare before them: and that which should have been for their welfare, let it become a trap” (Psa 69:22). The imprecation is not that the wicked lose their table but that the very thing they trusted for good should turn on them. Paul quotes it in Romans 11:9 and applies it to Israel's hardening: “Let their table be made a snare, and a trap, and a stumblingblock, and a recompence unto them” — the covenant privileges themselves, the law, the temple, the descent from Abraham, became the ground of a self-confidence that shut them out of the righteousness of faith. Blessings held apart from Christ turn into snares; that is the doctrine, and it is aimed as much at churches with a great heritage as at Israel. Jeremiah shows the human traps: “among my people are found wicked men: they lay wait, as he that setteth snares; they set a trap, they catch men” (Jer 5:26) — a fowler's language for men who prey on their neighbours, and the phrase they catch men is a dark echo of our Lord's promise to make fishers of men. And Bildad, describing the fate of the wicked: “The snare is laid for him in the ground, and a trap for him in the way” (Job 18:10).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines trap as an engine that shuts suddenly, used for taking game; and figuratively, an ambush, a stratagem, any thing by which one is caught unawares.

expand to see more

TRAP, n. An engine that shuts suddenly or with a spring, used for taking game.

1. An ambush; a stratagem; any device by which one is caught unawares.

TRAP, v.t. To catch in a trap; to insnare.

SNARE, n. An instrument for catching animals, particularly fowls, by the leg; anything by which one is entangled and brought into trouble.

Key Scripture

Psa 69:22 — "Let their table become a snare before them: and that which should have been for their welfare, let it become a trap."

Rom 11:9 — "And David saith, Let their table be made a snare, and a trap, and a stumblingblock, and a recompence unto them:"

Jer 5:26 — "For among my people are found wicked men: they lay wait, as he that setteth snares; they set a trap, they catch men."

Job 18:10 — "The snare is laid for him in the ground, and a trap for him in the way."

Modern Corruption

Inherited religious privilege is treated as security; Paul says the table itself became the trap.

expand to see more

Romans 11:9 is one of the most uncomfortable applications in Scripture, and it is aimed at the most privileged people in the world — those to whom pertain the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the service of God and the promises. The table that should have been for their welfare became a trap. The mechanism is not that the gifts were bad but that they were made the ground of confidence apart from the righteousness of God: they being ignorant of God's righteousness, and going about to establish their own righteousness, have not submitted themselves unto the righteousness of God (Rom 10:3). Every church with a great confession, a faithful history and a sound heritage should read that sentence slowly.

The passage also forbids the opposite error, and Paul spends the whole chapter on it. Gentile believers are told plainly not to boast against the branches — thou standest by faith. Be not highminded, but fear — because the God who did not spare the natural branches will not spare the grafted ones on any different terms. The trap and the graft are the same doctrine seen from two sides: no man stands on his privileges, and every man stands by faith alone.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew moqesh (H4170), a bait, a lure, a snare; pach (H6341), a bird-trap, a snare; Greek thera (G2339), a hunting, a prey, a trap.

expand to see more

Hebrew moqesh (H4170) — a bait or lure, the striker of a trap; Psalm 69:22, Job 18:10 — the word also used of idols as a snare to Israel.

Hebrew pach (H6341) — a bird-trap, a snare of the fowler; Psalm 91:3, 124:7.

Hebrew yaqush (H3353) — a fowler, one who sets snares; Jeremiah 5:26, as he that setteth snares.

Greek thera (G2339) — a hunting, a catching, a prey; Romans 11:9, rendered trap.

Greek skandalon (G4625) — the trigger-stick of a trap, a stumblingblock; the third word in Paul's chain.

Usage

"“That which should have been for their welfare, let it become a trap”."

"“Let their table be made a snare, and a trap” — the privileges themselves."

"“They set a trap, they catch men” — among God's own people."
